title: Children’s Headache Through Drawings: A Narrative Review and a Portrait Gallery
content:
Headache is one of the most common and debilitating conditions in pediatric age, compromising mental and psycho-logical health, as well as academic and social performance in children, significantly reducing the quality of life.
Currently, the diagnosis of headache is based on the clinical criteria of the third edition of the International Classifica-tion of Headache Disorders (ICHD-3). However, the characteristics of headache may differ between adults and children, as well as the ability of children to provide a complete description of the pain and associated symptoms.
The immature narrative skills of children can represent a limitation in defining the clinical phenotype of headache, making the diagnosis more complex. This is even more challenging when extracting information about the characteris-tics of the headache in children whose verbal expression is poorly developed or completely absent.
Given these limitations, clinical psychology has long used drawing, as an effective diagnostic instrument to bypass verbal communication barriers.
This tool provides unique access to children's psychological and emotional states, as a direct window into their inner world and as an expressive medium that often generate more detailed, accurate, and clinically actionable information, compared to verbal reports alone 
For these reasons, drawing has been recognized as a valuable diagnostic toolfor decades,with multiple studies demon-strating specificity and accuracy rates comparable to standard clinical assessments. Particularly for young childfren, drawings may give access to fundamental information that might otherwise remain inaccessible, , thereby allowing both accurate diagnosis and individualized treatment planning. 
Multiple studies have highlighted and confirmed the graphic differences between representations of various types of headaches and the undeniable utility of an "artistic diagnosis" alongside the clinical one.
Furthermore, the literature suggests and encourages the use of drawing in clinical practice, both in the diagnostic pro-cess and during subsequent follow-up, as an effective, enjoyable, easy-to-use, and low-cost resource.
Therefore, we propose a narrative review, accompanied by a collection of drawings, which may serve to identify and catalog the specific correlations between graphic representations and the characteristics of the clinical phenotype, such as pain location, quality, intensity, association with nausea and vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia, and types of migraine aura. The goal is to create a collection that can guide clinicians in the correct interpretation of the drawings.
In this review, we also aim to promote the integration of this approach into clinical practice to enhance diagnostic accu-racy and foster a more child-centered model of care.
